questions.q: Why does the lesson say an exposed AI API key is worse than a typical leaked credential?
options: It's effectively a payment method with no pre-set spending cap, attached to a compute-intensive product
AI API keys are always longer than other credentials
AI providers never allow keys to be rotated
AI API keys can only be used once and then expire automatically
questions.explain: The lesson frames an exposed AI API key as closer to a leaked payment method, since someone who finds it can run large bills quickly.

questions.q: What does the lesson identify as the most common way an AI API key leaks?
options: A sophisticated supply-chain attack on the AI provider
A brute-force password-guessing attack
A key embedded directly in client-side code, extractable from dev tools or a decompiled app
A compromised physical data center
questions.explain: The lesson calls client-side exposure the most common and entirely preventable leak path — not a sophisticated attack, just a five-minute discovery.

questions.q: According to the lesson, why is a key committed to git still a risk even after a later commit removes it?
options: Because GitHub automatically re-adds deleted keys
Because the key remains recoverable from git history unless the repository itself is rewritten
Because git automatically emails the key to attackers
It isn't a risk once removed in any later commit
questions.explain: The lesson explains that a committed key stays recoverable from git history even after a later commit appears to remove it.

questions.q: What is the lesson's recommended architectural fix for client-side key exposure?
options: Rename the key variable to something harder to guess
Encrypt the key using a password only the developer knows
The key should never leave the server — the browser calls your backend, and your backend calls the AI provider
Store the key in a longer string to make it harder to copy
questions.explain: The lesson describes the fix as architectural: proxy AI calls through your own backend so the key is never shipped to the client.

questions.q: Per the lesson, why do model weights themselves deserve the same access-control rigor as other sensitive assets?
options: Model weights have no real value and don't need protection
Model weights automatically delete themselves if accessed improperly
They are legally required to be public
They encode training effort and sometimes proprietary data or trade secrets, making them a theft target
questions.explain: The lesson notes that for teams hosting or fine-tuning their own models, the weights are valuable intellectual property and need the same access rigor as any other high-value asset.
